question: What datasets did the authors use for their experiments and how large were they in terms of samples and dimensionality? Did they use the raw data or did they apply any preprocessing or augmentation?
answer:
Based on the provided context, the authors evaluated their models across seven datasets spanning vision, speech, text, and genetics domains. Table 1 in (1) details their input dimensionality and training/test set sizes:

- **MNIST**: Vision, 784-dim (28×28 grayscale), 60K training / 10K test samples
- **SVHN**: Vision, 3,072-dim (32×32 color), 600K training / 26K test samples
- **CIFAR-10/100**: Vision, 3,072-dim (32×32 color), 60K training / 10K test samples
- **ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012)**: Vision, 65,536-dim (256×256 color), 1.2M training / 150K test samples
- **TIMIT**: Speech, 2,520-dim (120-dim over 21 frames), 1.1M training / 58K test frames
- **Reuters-RCV1**: Text, 2,000-dim, 200K training / 200K test samples
- **Alternative Splicing**: Genetics, 1,014-dim, 2,932 training / 733 test samples

Regarding preprocessing and augmentation, the authors explicitly state that no data augmentation was applied to CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 apart from input dropout (2, 3). They also note that leveraging 2-D spatial information and augmenting training sets with distorted images could potentially yield better results on image tasks (4), but the provided excerpt does not detail additional preprocessing or augmentation steps applied to any of the other datasets.

6.1.3 CIF AR-10 and CIF AR-100 The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 data sets consist of 32 × 32 color images drawn from 10 and 100 categories respectively. Figure 5b shows some examples of images from this data set. A detailed description of the data sets, input preprocessing, network architectures and other experimental details is given in Appendix B.3. Table 4 shows the error rate obtained by different methods on these data sets. Without any data augmentation, Snoek et al. (2012) used Bayesian hyperparameter optimization to obtained an error rate of 14.98% on CIFAR-10. Using dropout in the fully connected layers reduces that to 14.32% and adding dropout in every layer further reduces the error to 12.61%. Goodfellow et al. (2013) showed that the error is further reduced to 11.68% by replacing ReLU units with maxout units.

Goodfellow et al. (2013) showed that the error is further reduced to 11.68% by replacing ReLU units with maxout units. On CIFAR-100, dropout reduces the error from 43.48% to 37.20% which is a huge improvement. No data augmentation was used for either data set (apart from the input dropout).

Dropout nets pretrained with stacks of RBMs and Deep Boltzmann Machines also give improvements as shown in Table 2. DBM—pretrained dropout nets achieve a test error of 0.79% which is the best performance ever reported for the permutation invariant setting. We note that it possible to obtain better results by using 2-D spatial information and augmenting the training set with distorted versions of images from the standard training set. We demonstrate the effectiveness of dropout in that setting on more interesting data sets.
